paragraphs.title: Punishment and the Call to Repentance

easy.explanation: The verse says, “O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God.”
easy.q: Who is told to return to the LORD?

easy.explanation: Israel has fallen because of its iniquity.
Israel is called to return to the LORD its God.
easy.q: To whom is Israel called to return?

answers: The fall leads Israel to return to the LORD
The fall causes Israel to trust Assyria
The fall leads Israel to worship idols
medium.explanation: Israel’s fall because of iniquity is followed by a call to return to God.
medium.q: What is the relationship between Israel’s fall and the call to return?
What does “iniquity” mean in this passage?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “thou hast fallen by thine iniquity.”
medium.q: What does the passage present as the result of Israel’s sin?

answers: The passage moves from falling in sin to returning to God
The passage moves from harvest to war
The passage moves from worship to military victory
challenge.explanation: The first verse describes Israel’s fall, while the next calls Israel to return.
challenge.q: What change takes place between the two verses?

challenge.explanation: Returning to the LORD implies turning back to Him in repentance.
challenge.q: What does “return unto the LORD thy God” imply?

answers: Iniquity leads to falling, while repentance leads back to God
Harvest leads to sin, while sin leads to peace
Military power leads to worship, while worship leads to exile
challenge.explanation: Israel’s iniquity causes its fall, and the call to return points it back to God.
challenge.q: Which cause-and-effect relationship fits the passage?

paragraphs.title: Confession, Reliance on God, and Rejection of False Supports

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Take with you words.”
easy.q: What are the people told to take with them?

easy.explanation: Israel says, “Asshur shall not save us.”
easy.q: What does Israel say Asshur will not do?

easy.explanation: Israel will no longer say to the work of its hands, “Ye are our gods.”
easy.q: What will Israel no longer call the work of its hands?

medium.explanation: “The calves of our lips” represents worship and confession offered through words.
medium.q: What is offered in place of animal sacrifices?

medium.explanation: Israel asks God to remove its sin.
medium.q: What does “Take away all iniquity” express?

answers: Returning, confessing, and rejecting false supports
medium.explanation: Israel is told to return, speak words of confession, and reject false sources of security.
medium.q: What sequence appears in these verses?

answers: They are symbols of Israel’s harvest
challenge.explanation: Israel rejects political help from Asshur, military strength represented by horses, and handmade idols.
challenge.q: What do Asshur, horses, and idols have in common?

answers: Repentance includes confession and a change of trust
challenge.explanation: Israel confesses its sin and stops relying on false supports.
challenge.q: What understanding of repentance is shown here?

challenge.explanation: The verse says, “in thee the fatherless findeth mercy,” referring to the LORD.
challenge.q: Who shows mercy to the fatherless?

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “I will heal their backsliding.”
easy.q: What does the LORD promise to do for Israel’s backsliding?
What flower is used to describe Israel’s growth?

easy.explanation: They “shall return” and “revive as the corn.”
easy.q: What happens to those who dwell under Israel’s shadow?

answers: Healing leads to growth and blessing
Healing leads to falling in battle
medium.explanation: After healing and love are promised, the passage describes dew, flowers, roots, branches, grain, and vines.
medium.q: What is the relationship between healing and flourishing?

answers: The LORD will love them generously and willingly
The LORD will love them because of military power
The LORD will love them only because they are wealthy
medium.explanation: The phrase describes freely given, gracious love.
medium.q: What does “I will love them freely” mean?

answers: Dew, growth, roots, spreading branches, and fruit
medium.explanation: The imagery moves from dew and growth to roots, branches, shade, and fruit.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the plant imagery?

challenge.explanation: Deep roots suggest stability, strength, and lasting renewal.
challenge.q: What does casting forth roots as Lebanon suggest?

answers: Lily, olive tree, corn, and vine
challenge.explanation: The passage uses plant, grain, and vine imagery to portray flourishing.
challenge.q: Which group contains most of the passage’s images of prosperity?

answers: Renewal blesses both Israel and others
challenge.explanation: Israel is renewed and becomes fruitful, giving shade and blessing to others.
challenge.q: What does the movement from healing to shade and fruit show?

paragraphs.title: God as the Source of Fruit and the Meaning of His Ways

easy.explanation: Ephraim asks, “What have I to do any more with idols?”
easy.q: What does Ephraim ask to leave behind?

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “From me is thy fruit found.”
easy.q: Who is the source of Ephraim’s fruit?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “the ways of the LORD are right.”
easy.q: How are the ways of the LORD described?

answers: The LORD is the source of Ephraim’s fruitfulness
medium.explanation: The LORD identifies Himself as the source of Ephraim’s fruit.
medium.q: What does “From me is thy fruit found” mean?

medium.explanation: Idols are objects worshiped as false gods.
medium.q: What does “idols” mean in this context?

answers: The just walk in them, but transgressors fall in them
Transgressors walk in them, but the just fall
medium.explanation: The verse says, “the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall therein.”
medium.q: How do the just and transgressors respond to the ways of the LORD?

answers: The LORD’s ways are right, but people respond to them differently
The LORD’s ways are hidden, so everyone falls
The LORD’s ways lead everyone to idols
challenge.explanation: The ways of the LORD are right, yet the just walk in them while transgressors fall.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast at the end of the passage?

answers: Recognizing God as the source leads to understanding His ways
challenge.explanation: The passage calls people to recognize God as the source of fruit and to understand His right ways.
challenge.q: What idea connects the source of fruit with the LORD’s ways?

answers: Understanding is needed to recognize the meaning of God’s ways
No one needs to understand God’s ways
challenge.explanation: The closing questions emphasize wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of the LORD’s ways.
challenge.q: What does the question “Who is wise, and he shall understand these things?” emphasize?
